analogy.p: Picture a **giant steel chain-link fence** made of millions of links, each joined to its neighbours: to pull the fence apart you must break an enormous number of links, which is like breaking the covalent bonds in **diamond**, so it is very hard and has a very high melting point. Now picture **a stack of separate chain-link mats** lying on top of each other: each mat is strong, but the mats slide over one another very easily, like the layers of **graphite**. The analogy breaks down because in graphite the layers are held together by weak forces of attraction between atoms, not by loose stacking, and the delocalised electrons that allow graphite to conduct have no equivalent in a fence.
analogy.t: A chain-link fence versus a stack of chain-link mats

bullets: Know that giant covalent structures are **solids at room temperature** with **very high melting points**.
Explain the high melting point as: **many strong covalent bonds** must be **broken** (overcome), which takes a **lot of energy**.
Know the three examples: **diamond**, **graphite** and **silicon dioxide**.
Explain differences between diamond and graphite using the number of bonds per carbon atom and the presence of delocalised electrons.
Use models (ball and stick, 2D and 3D diagrams) to represent the structures and say what their limitations are.
Compare giant covalent substances with simple molecular, ionic and metallic substances (links to 4.2.1 and 4.2.2 in the same chapter).
Expect marks from 1 mark recall (name an example) up to 4 to 6 mark questions where you must explain properties using bonding.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8462 section 4.2.2 says that substances with **giant covalent structures** are **solids with very high melting points**. All of the atoms in these structures are **linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds**, and these bonds **must be overcome to melt or boil** these substances. The three examples you must know are **diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide**. The skill that earns the marks is not just stating the properties but **linking each property to the structure and bonding**, and being able to recognise a giant covalent substance from a table of data.

bullets: Made of **non-metal atoms** only, joined by **strong covalent bonds** (shared pairs of electrons).
The atoms form a **regular repeating lattice**: every atom is bonded to its neighbours, which are bonded to their neighbours, and so on.
There are **no individual molecules**, so you cannot give a molecular formula. The formula shows the **simplest whole-number ratio** of atoms (the empirical formula), e.g. SiO₂.
Diamond and graphite are both made of **only carbon atoms**; silicon dioxide has **silicon and oxygen atoms** in a 1 : 2 ratio.

A **simple molecular** substance has small molecules with strong covalent bonds **inside** each molecule but weak **intermolecular forces** between them; a giant covalent substance has strong covalent bonds **all the way through**.
Link to other topics: the same ideas are used for **graphene and fullerenes** (4.2.4) and for the **bonding types** summary (4.2.1).
core.h: What a giant covalent structure is
core.p: In a **giant covalent structure** (also called a **giant covalent lattice** or **macromolecule**) a huge number of atoms are joined together by **covalent bonds** in a continuous network. A **covalent bond** is a **shared pair of electrons** between two non-metal atoms. In a simple molecule such as water the covalent bonds join only a few atoms into a small unit. In a giant structure there are no separate small units: the bonding goes on and on in all directions (or across whole layers in graphite), so the whole crystal is effectively one enormous molecule.

bullets: Say: the **strong covalent bonds** between the atoms must be **overcome/broken**, which requires a **lot of energy**.
Do not say 'intermolecular forces' for diamond or silicon dioxide, because there are **no molecules**.

Compare: **simple molecular** substances (e.g. water, methane) have **low** melting points because only **weak intermolecular forces** need to be overcome; the covalent bonds inside the molecules stay intact.

**Ionic** compounds also have high melting points because of strong **electrostatic forces** between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice, but they conduct when molten, unlike most giant covalent substances.
Boiling points are also **very high** for the same reason: the bonds must be overcome to turn the substance to a gas.

Approximate values (do not need to learn exactly): **diamond and graphite above 3500 °C** (graphite changes directly to a gas rather than melting at normal pressure); **silicon dioxide about 1700 °C**.
core.h: Why the melting points are so high
core.p: To **melt** a solid the particles must gain enough energy to break free from their fixed positions. In a giant covalent substance the particles are **atoms held by strong covalent bonds**, so to melt or boil it you must **break (overcome) these covalent bonds**, not just weak forces between molecules. Covalent bonds are very strong and there are **huge numbers of them** to break, so a **very large amount of energy** is needed. This is why diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide are solids with very high melting points. Always say **bonds are broken**, not that molecules are separated.

bullets: Carbon is in **Group 4** (four electrons in its outer shell), so each atom needs to share four electrons: **four covalent bonds per atom**.
The bonds are arranged **tetrahedrally** with bond angles of **109.5°**, making a strong, rigid **3D lattice**.
**Every outer electron is used** in a bond, so there are **no delocalised electrons**.
The structure is the same in all directions, so diamond is equally hard whichever way it is cut, but it is **brittle** along certain planes (it can be cleaved by a sharp blow in the right place).
Diamond is one **allotrope** of carbon (the same element in different structural forms); others are graphite, graphene and fullerenes.
In diagrams the carbon atoms are shown as balls and the covalent bonds as sticks (**ball and stick model**).
core.p: In **diamond** each carbon atom forms **four covalent bonds** with four other carbon atoms. The four bonds point towards the corners of a **tetrahedron**, so the arrangement is a rigid **three-dimensional giant covalent structure** that extends in all directions. All of the outer-shell electrons of each carbon atom are used in bonding, so none are free to move. Every carbon atom is held in a fixed position by four strong bonds, which gives diamond its remarkable properties.

bullets: **Very hard**: each atom has **four strong covalent bonds** in a rigid 3D lattice, so atoms cannot be moved apart or slid easily. (Diamond is the hardest natural substance.)
**Very high melting point**: many **strong covalent bonds** must be broken, needing a lot of energy.
**Does not conduct electricity**: all four outer electrons of each carbon are in covalent bonds, so there are **no delocalised electrons** and no ions to carry charge.
**Insoluble in water** and most solvents: the strong bonds in the lattice are not broken by solvent molecules.
**Uses**: **cutting tools, drill bits and saws** (hardness), **jewellery** (sparkles because of how it refracts light and because it is hard wearing).
Stick to the three properties the specification links to structure: hardness, melting point and (lack of) electrical conductivity.
core.p: Each property of diamond follows directly from its structure. Because each atom is held by **four strong covalent bonds** in a rigid lattice, a very large force is needed to push atoms past each other or to break the bonds, so diamond is **very hard** and has a **very high melting point**. It **does not conduct electricity** because there are **no free (delocalised) electrons or ions** to carry a charge. When answering, always give the property, the structural reason, and the effect.

bullets: **Three covalent bonds** per carbon atom, giving flat **hexagonal rings** joined into layers.
**No covalent bonds between layers**: only **weak intermolecular forces**, so the layers are far apart compared with the bond length inside a layer.
**One delocalised electron per carbon atom**: the fourth outer electron is not used in bonding and is free to move.
The structure is therefore **layered** (2D sheets stacked in 3D), unlike diamond which is bonded equally in all directions.
Graphite is another **allotrope of carbon**. A **single layer** of graphite is called **graphene** (4.2.4).
Draw graphite as stacked layers of hexagons with dotted or dashed lines between the layers to show the weak forces.
core.p: In **graphite** each carbon atom forms **three covalent bonds** with three other carbon atoms. These bonds make **layers of hexagonal rings** of carbon atoms. There are **no covalent bonds between the layers**; instead there are only **weak intermolecular forces** holding the layers together. Because each carbon uses only three of its four outer electrons for bonding, **one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised** and free to move through the structure.

bullets: **Soft and slippery**: the layers are held by **weak forces**, so they **slide over each other easily**.
**Conducts electricity**: **one delocalised electron per carbon atom** is free to move and carry charge. Graphite is a non-metal that conducts.
**Very high melting point**: the **strong covalent bonds** within the layers must be overcome. (It is not the weak forces between layers that matter for melting.)
**Uses**: **electrodes** in electrolysis (it conducts and is unreactive and has a high melting point), **lubricant** (layers slide), **pencil 'lead'** (layers rub off onto paper).
**Less dense than diamond** because the layers are spaced far apart.
Compare in one sentence: 'Graphite conducts because it has delocalised electrons, whereas diamond does not because all its outer electrons are in covalent bonds.'
core.p: Graphite behaves very differently from diamond even though both are pure carbon, and this is a favourite exam comparison. The **layers can slide over each other** because only weak intermolecular forces hold them together, which makes graphite **soft and slippery**. It **conducts electricity** because of the **delocalised electrons** that can move through the structure and carry charge. It still has a **very high melting point** because the **strong covalent bonds** inside each layer must be broken.

bullets: Each **Si** forms **four covalent bonds**, one to each of four oxygen atoms.
Each **O** forms **two covalent bonds**, one to each of two silicon atoms.

The **ratio of silicon to oxygen is 1 : 2** because each silicon has 4 bonds to oxygen, and each oxygen is shared between 2 silicon atoms, so each Si has 4 × ½ = **2 O atoms**. This is why the formula is **SiO₂**.
The formula SiO₂ is an **empirical formula**, not a molecule; there are no separate SiO₂ molecules.
It is a **3D network of strong covalent bonds** with **no delocalised electrons and no ions**.
Do not confuse with **carbon dioxide (CO₂)**, which is a **simple molecule** (a gas) with a very low melting point.
core.p: **Silicon dioxide** (also called **silica**, SiO₂) is the main compound in **sand** and in the mineral **quartz**. It is a **giant covalent structure** in which each **silicon atom is covalently bonded to four oxygen atoms**, and each **oxygen atom is bonded to two silicon atoms**. The structure is a continuous three-dimensional network. It is similar in shape to diamond, with oxygen atoms placed between the silicon atoms.

bullets: **High melting point and boiling point**: strong covalent bonds throughout the giant structure must be broken.
**Hard** and **brittle**: strong bonds hold the atoms rigidly in place, but a sharp force can fracture the crystal.
**Does not conduct electricity** (solid or liquid): no delocalised electrons and no free ions.
**Uses**: **sand** is used in building materials such as mortar and concrete; silicon dioxide is the main raw material for making **glass** (sand is heated with other substances).

A commonly asked comparison: silicon dioxide (a giant covalent solid) versus **carbon dioxide** (a gas) even though both have the formula type XO₂: the structure, not the formula, decides the properties.
Silicon dioxide is **insoluble in water**, like diamond, because water molecules cannot overcome its strong covalent bonds.
core.p: Silicon dioxide has a **high melting point (about 1700 °C)** because many strong covalent bonds must be broken. It is **hard** and **does not conduct electricity** because it has no delocalised electrons or ions. It is **insoluble in water**. These properties make it useful in the construction and glass industries.

bullets: **Diamond**: does not conduct, because **no delocalised electrons**.
**Silicon dioxide**: does not conduct, because **no delocalised electrons** and **no ions**.
**Graphite**: conducts, because **one delocalised electron per carbon atom** is free to move.
**Ionic compounds** conduct only when **molten or dissolved**, because the ions are then free to move; as solids the ions are fixed.
**Metals** conduct as solids and liquids because of **delocalised electrons** (see Metals and alloys).
Exam phrase for 2 marks: '**free (delocalised) electrons** that can **carry charge**'. Do not say 'electrons are free' without saying they carry charge.
core.h: Electrical conductivity of giant covalent substances
core.p: For a substance to conduct electricity it needs **charged particles that are free to move**: either **delocalised electrons** (as in metals and graphite) or **mobile ions** (as in molten or dissolved ionic compounds). Diamond and silicon dioxide have neither, so they **do not conduct** in any state. Graphite has delocalised electrons, so it **conducts as a solid**. This is the only common non-metal element you must know that conducts electricity.

bullets: **Simple molecular** (e.g. water, methane, carbon dioxide): **low melting and boiling points** (weak intermolecular forces), **do not conduct**, often gases or liquids.
**Ionic** (e.g. sodium chloride): **high melting point**, **conduct when molten or dissolved** but not as solids, many dissolve in water.
**Giant covalent** (diamond, silicon dioxide): **very high melting point**, **do not conduct**, insoluble. **Graphite** is the exception that **conducts**.
**Metallic**: **high melting point** (most), **conduct as solids**, **malleable**.
To identify: **very high melting point + no conduction** points to **giant covalent**; **high mp + conducts only when molten** points to **ionic**.
Always back up the identification with **bonding**: 'strong covalent bonds throughout' or 'strong electrostatic forces between ions'.
core.h: Comparing the four types of structure
core.p: Exam questions often give you data about unfamiliar substances and ask you to decide what type of structure each has. Use **melting point, conductivity and solubility** as clues. Giant covalent substances stand out because they have **very high melting points** and **do not conduct** (except graphite), and they are **insoluble**. Learn this table of patterns and apply it with reasons from the bonding.

bullets: **Ball and stick model**: shows the **3D arrangement, bond angles and the number of bonds**; the balls are much smaller than real atoms and the sticks suggest bonds are physical rods.
**2D diagram**: easy to draw but the 3D shape of diamond and silicon dioxide is **lost**, and bond angles look wrong.
**Space-filling model**: shows relative atom sizes but **hides the bonds** and the inner atoms.
None of the models can show the **whole giant structure**; they show a small section that **repeats** (use dashed lines or dots to show it continues).
When drawing: label **carbon atoms**, show **4 bonds on each carbon for diamond**, **3 bonds in hexagons for graphite**, and **layers** with weak forces between them.
State a limitation in exams: 'it does not show that the structure continues in all directions' or 'bonds are not real sticks'.
core.h: Representing the structures: models and their limits
core.p: AQA expects you to **represent giant covalent structures using ball and stick models** and to say what is good and bad about each type of model. A **ball and stick** model shows atoms as balls and bonds as sticks, so you can see the **number of bonds, the angles and the 3D arrangement**. A **2D diagram** is quicker to draw but cannot show the third dimension properly, and a **dot and cross diagram** is unsuitable for a giant structure because there are too many atoms.

bullets: **Graphene** is a **single layer of graphite**, one atom thick; it is very strong and conducts because it keeps the delocalised electrons (see Diamond, graphite, graphene and fullerenes).
**Electrolysis**: graphite is used for **electrodes** because it conducts, has a high melting point and is relatively unreactive.
**Empirical formula** skills link: SiO₂ is the simplest ratio of Si : O atoms in the network.
**Particle model**: giant covalent solids do not change state easily because covalent bonds must break, unlike simple molecular substances where only intermolecular forces break.

**Predicting properties**: if a question gives a new giant covalent substance, say 'it will have a high melting point because strong covalent bonds must be broken', and decide on conductivity from whether any electrons are delocalised.
In calculations or data questions, check the **units of temperature (°C)** and compare numbers carefully.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher-level thinking
core.p: Giant covalent structures link to **allotropes of carbon** (graphene and fullerenes), **electrolysis** (graphite electrodes), and to **properties of materials** in the Using Resources topic. At higher grades you are expected to reason from unfamiliar data and to give **precise, causal explanations**, not lists of properties.

exam: **1 mark (State/Name)**: give the exact word, e.g. 'diamond', 'graphite', 'silicon dioxide', 'delocalised electron'.

**Explain high melting point (2 to 3 marks)**: (1) giant covalent structure/lattice with many covalent bonds; (2) strong covalent bonds must be broken/overcome; (3) a lot of energy is needed. Never write 'intermolecular forces' for diamond or silicon dioxide.
**Explain why diamond is hard (2 marks)**: each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds (1) in a rigid giant lattice which atoms cannot slide past/strong bonds hard to break (1).
**Explain why graphite conducts (2 marks)**: each carbon forms three bonds so one electron is delocalised (1); delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge (1).
**Explain why graphite is soft/slippery (2 marks)**: layers of atoms with no covalent bonds between the layers (1); weak intermolecular forces so layers slide over each other (1).

**Compare diamond and graphite (4 marks)**: bonds per atom (4 v 3), structure (3D lattice v layers), delocalised electrons (none v one each), consequence (hard, non-conductor v soft, conductor). Use 'whereas' to link both sides.

**Identify substances from data**: very high melting point + does not conduct = giant covalent; high melting point + conducts when molten/dissolved only = ionic; low melting point + does not conduct = simple molecular. Quote the figures.
**Silicon dioxide formula (2 marks)**: each Si is bonded to 4 O; each O is shared between 2 Si; so 1 Si : 2 O, SiO₂.
**Models (2 marks)**: ball and stick shows the 3D arrangement/bond angles; limitation is that it does not show the structure continues, or bonds are not real sticks.

**Command words**: State = short fact; Describe = say what the structure is like; Explain = give a reason using because/so; Compare = similarities and differences together; Suggest = apply your knowledge to something unfamiliar.

**6 mark extended answer**: structure it as (1) type of structure and bonding, (2) number of bonds per atom, (3) melting point explained, (4) electrical conductivity explained, (5) hardness or softness explained, (6) uses linked to properties; finish with a conclusion sentence.

mistakes.r: Diamond has no molecules; the strong covalent bonds between atoms must be broken (overcome), which needs a lot of energy.
mistakes.w: To melt diamond, you break the intermolecular forces between molecules.

mistakes.r: Diamond does not conduct because all four outer electrons of each carbon are used in covalent bonds, so there are no delocalised electrons.
mistakes.w: Diamond has a high melting point because of strong covalent bonds, so it conducts electricity.

mistakes.r: Covalent bonds are strong. Graphite is soft because there are only weak intermolecular forces between the layers, so the layers slide over each other.
mistakes.w: Graphite is soft because it has weak covalent bonds.

mistakes.r: Graphite has a very high melting point because the strong covalent bonds within the layers must be broken.
mistakes.w: Graphite has a low melting point because its layers slide.

mistakes.r: Graphite conducts because one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised and can move and carry charge.
mistakes.w: Graphite conducts because it has ions.

mistakes.r: Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure; SiO₂ is just the simplest ratio of Si to O. Carbon dioxide is a small molecule.
mistakes.w: Silicon dioxide is made of SiO₂ molecules, like CO₂.

mistakes.r: Each carbon in graphite forms three covalent bonds (hexagons); in diamond it is four.
mistakes.w: Each carbon in graphite is bonded to four atoms.

mistakes.r: Only graphite does (delocalised electrons). Diamond and silicon dioxide do not.
mistakes.w: All giant covalent substances conduct electricity.

mistakes.r: Giant covalent substances are insoluble in water because their strong covalent bonds are not overcome by water molecules.
mistakes.w: A giant covalent substance dissolves in water because it has strong bonds.

summary: AQA 4.2.2: substances with giant covalent structures are solids with very high melting points because all the atoms are linked by strong covalent bonds that must be overcome to melt or boil them. You must know the structures, properties and uses of diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide, and explain differences (such as why graphite conducts but diamond does not) using bonding. It matters because bonding-to-property explanations are tested in almost every Chemistry paper.

terms.d: A structure in which a very large number of atoms are linked by strong covalent bonds in a continuous network; these substances are solids with very high melting points.
A shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms.
A giant molecule or lattice made of a very large number of atoms bonded covalently.
A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with four other carbon atoms in a giant covalent structure.
A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds, giving layers of hexagonal rings with no covalent bonds between the layers; one electron from each atom is delocalised.
A giant covalent compound (SiO₂, silica) in which each silicon atom bonds to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom bonds to two silicon atoms; the main compound in sand.
Different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state, e.g. diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon.
An electron that is not bound to one atom or bond and is free to move through the structure, able to carry charge.
Weak forces of attraction between molecules (or between layers in graphite); they are much weaker than covalent bonds.
A 3D arrangement in which a central atom has four bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, as in diamond (bond angle 109.5°).
Rings of six carbon atoms joined together; they make the flat layers in graphite and graphene.
A 3D model in which atoms are shown as balls and covalent bonds as sticks.
The simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound, e.g. SiO₂ for silicon dioxide.
A regular repeating arrangement of particles in a solid.
The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid; the particles gain enough energy to overcome the forces holding them in place.
A conducting rod, often graphite or metal, through which electricity enters or leaves an electrolyte in electrolysis.

worked.ans: Model answer: Diamond is a giant covalent structure with each carbon atom joined to four others by strong covalent bonds. A lot of energy is needed to break (overcome) these many strong covalent bonds, so it has a very high melting point.
worked.q: Diamond has a very high melting point of over 3500 °C. Explain why, in terms of its structure and bonding. (3 marks)
steps: Name the structure: diamond is a giant covalent structure (macromolecule) in which each carbon atom is bonded to four others.
State what happens on melting: the strong covalent bonds between the atoms must be broken/overcome.
Link to energy: there are very many strong bonds, so a lot of energy is needed.

worked.ans: Model answer: Graphite is a good lubricant because its layers are held by weak forces so they slide over each other. It is a good electrode because each carbon has one delocalised electron that can move and carry charge, and its strong covalent bonds give it a high melting point.
worked.q: Graphite is used as a lubricant and as an electrode. Explain how its structure makes it suitable for each use. (4 marks)
steps: Lubricant: graphite has layers of carbon atoms in hexagonal rings with no covalent bonds between the layers (1).
Only weak intermolecular forces hold the layers together, so the layers can slide over each other (1).
Electrode: each carbon is bonded to only three others, so one electron per atom is delocalised (1).
These delocalised electrons are free to move through the graphite and carry electric charge (1).

worked.ans: (a) Each Si bonds to 4 O and each O is shared between 2 Si, so the ratio Si : O is 1 : 2, giving SiO₂. (b) SiO₂ is a giant covalent structure so many strong covalent bonds must be broken (a lot of energy). CO₂ is a simple molecule so only weak intermolecular forces are overcome (little energy).
worked.q: Silicon dioxide has the formula SiO₂. (a) Explain why the formula is SiO₂ using the bonding in the structure. (b) Explain why silicon dioxide has a high melting point but carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature. (5 marks)
steps: (a) Each silicon atom is covalently bonded to four oxygen atoms (1).
Each oxygen atom is bonded to two silicon atoms, so each oxygen is shared by two Si; per silicon that is 4 × ½ = 2 oxygen atoms, giving a 1 : 2 ratio (1).
(b) Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure, so many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it, which needs a lot of energy (1).
Carbon dioxide is a simple molecular substance, so only weak intermolecular forces must be overcome to separate the molecules (1).
These need little energy, so carbon dioxide has a very low melting point and is a gas at room temperature (1).
